prompt: A team announces two weeks of "refactoring the payments module", during which the module will not work. What is it doing, in Fowler's terms?

choices.text: Refactoring, since the internal structure is what changes
choices.why: Structure changing is half of the definition; the other half is that the program works after every small step.

choices.text: A rewrite: one large step nobody runs until it ends
choices.why: Right. Refactoring is a chain of small behaviour-preserving moves, and you can stop at any of them with a working program.

choices.text: Refactoring, as long as the tests pass at the end of the two weeks
choices.why: Green at the end of a fortnight says nothing about the fortnight; the point is green after every move.

prompt: A commit renames half of a module and also changes how fines are calculated. What is wrong with it?

choices.text: Renames should never be committed; editors redo them on demand
choices.why: Renames are ordinary refactorings and belong in history like any other change.

choices.text: Nothing, if the tests were updated to match the new fines
choices.why: Updated tests pass, and nobody can tell from them whether the renames changed behaviour too.

choices.text: Both hats at once: if something breaks, nobody knows which half did it
choices.why: Right. Adding behaviour and refactoring alternate; mixed in one change, neither can be reviewed or blamed.

choices.text: It is too small: refactorings should be batched into one weekly commit
choices.why: Small and frequent is the point of refactoring; batching is how a refactoring turns into a rewrite.

prompt: Match each smell to the move that usually fixes it.

pairs.left: repeated switches on a type code

prompt: A test that records what legacy code does today, right or wrong, is what Feathers calls a ___ test.
Put the steps for pinning down what an untested branch prints in the order the section takes them.
items: Write the assertion with an answer you know is wrong
Run it and read the actual value in the failure
Copy that value into the test
Run again and see it pass
trap: Guessing the right value first skips the point: the code, not you, says what it does.

prompt: The characterisation tests show that a month with nobody late prints "total: R$ 0,00", and a librarian says it should print nothing. What now?

choices.text: Fix it during the next refactoring, since the file is open anyway
choices.why: A behaviour change inside a refactoring is the two-hats mistake; the tests could no longer tell them apart.

choices.text: Make it a separate change with its own test and commit
choices.why: Right. The test records what is, and changing what is gets its own red, green and review.

choices.text: Delete the test, because it is wrong
choices.why: The test is an accurate record; deleting it removes the net without fixing the behaviour.

prompt: What is Fowler's test for whether a block should be extracted into a function?

choices.text: It is longer than ten lines
choices.why: Length is not the criterion; a one-line expression can deserve a name.

choices.text: You have to read it to know what it is for
choices.why: Right. Intention, not size: a name that says what it is for saves every later reader the reading.

choices.text: It is used in more than one place in the module
choices.why: That is the duplication case; a block used once can still be worth extracting.

choices.text: A profiler shows that most of the run time is spent inside it
choices.why: Extraction is about reading, not speed, and it does not make code faster.

prompt: Four lines of if l[6]: end = l[6] else: end = today became end = row[6] or today. Why was that safe here?

choices.text: or always behaves exactly like if/else in Python
choices.why: Not always: for a value that could be 0 or an empty string, or would pick today where the if picked the value.

choices.text: A date is never false, so both forms agree
choices.why: Right. The field is a date or None, and only None is false among those.

choices.text: The tests covered it, so any rewrite of those lines was safe
choices.why: Tests catch what they reach; the reasoning about dates is what makes this one safe for values no test tried.

prompt: Above a block in a long function sits the comment # work out when it is due. What does the section read that as?

choices.text: A function name written in the wrong place
choices.why: Right. Extract the block as due_date and the comment has nothing left to say.

choices.text: Good documentation, which makes extraction unnecessary
choices.why: The comment explains the block and still leaves the reader inside a function doing several jobs.

choices.text: A sign the block is too short to deserve a function
choices.why: Shortness never disqualifies a block; an unclear purpose is what qualifies it.

prompt: Why is the money formatting written twice in the legacy report a risk, if both copies are correct today?

choices.text: Two copies make the program slower to run
choices.why: The cost is not speed; it is the change that updates one copy and not the other.

choices.text: A later change will update one copy and quietly miss the other
choices.why: Right. Add a thousands separator and only the line somebody complained about gets it.

choices.text: Python refuses to compile a module that repeats an expression
choices.why: Python accepts any amount of repetition; it ran for years like that.

prompt: Books are lent for 14 days and films for 7. A colleague suggests FILM_DAYS = BOOK_DAYS // 2 to remove the "duplication". What does the section say?

choices.text: Good: one number to change instead of two
choices.why: Change the book loan to 21 days and films silently become 10, which nobody decided.

choices.text: Good, as long as the characterisation tests still pass
choices.why: They pass today because 14 // 2 is 7; the coupling only shows up on the day one policy changes.

choices.text: Wrong: they are two policies, not one fact
choices.why: Right. DRY is about knowledge; text or numbers that look alike can still be independent decisions.

prompt: Dropping :02d from money() turned R$ 2,00 into R$ 2,0. What caught it?

choices.text: A code review, which spotted the missing zero
choices.why: The section argues the opposite: R$ 2,0 looks plausible to a reader.

choices.text: Python, which rejects an f-string format without a width
choices.why: Without :02d the f-string is valid and simply prints 0 instead of 00.

choices.text: The approved output, compared byte for byte by the tests
choices.why: Right. Both tests failed within a second, naming the lines that differed.

prompt: After the move to Money, what happens to Money(50) + 3?

choices.text: It returns Money(53), adding the cents
choices.why: __add__ reads other.cents, which an int does not have.

choices.text: It always raises an AttributeError
choices.why: Right. Adding a count to money is now loud instead of quietly wrong.

choices.text: It returns 53, an int, like the old code
choices.why: The old code would have; that silent wrong number is what the class removes.

prompt: Why did the row become a NamedTuple rather than a new class that callers construct?

choices.text: NamedTuple is faster than any class
choices.why: Speed was never the reason given; keeping the interface was.

choices.text: Because a dataclass cannot hold a date | None field
choices.why: Loan in the next section is a dataclass with exactly that field.

choices.text: It names positions yet stays a tuple, so callers are untouched
choices.why: Right. Row._make wraps the incoming tuple; report(rows, today) did not change for anyone.

choices.text: So that row[4] keeps working inside report
choices.why: The point was the opposite: inside, row[4] became row.kind.

prompt: The library only ever prints members' phone numbers. Should phone become a PhoneNumber class now?

choices.text: Not yet: it carries no rules, so a string is all it needs
choices.why: Right. Wrap a primitive when it has behaviour to hold; validating or dialling would earn the class.

choices.text: Yes: every domain value must have its own type
choices.why: That is wrapping as a ritual, which the section warns against.

choices.text: Yes, because strings cannot hold the + sign of +55
choices.why: A string holds any character; the + is printed in the data already.

prompt: What is Fowler's test for whether a group of values is a data clump?

choices.text: They have the same type
choices.why: Name and phone are both strings and the date is not; type is not what makes them one thing.

choices.text: Delete one in your head: do the others still make sense alone?
choices.why: Right. A phone number without its person is useless, so name, phone and email are a member.

choices.text: They appear in alphabetical order in the tuple
choices.why: Order in a tuple is an accident, and the clump is about meaning.

choices.text: They are all read by one function at least once in the module
choices.why: One function reading several fields is closer to envy; the clump test asks whether they mean anything apart.

prompt: Put the moves of the section in the order it gives, each followed by a test run.
items: Introduce Member and build it in report
Introduce Loan with from_row, kind still a string
Add contact() and use it in the f-string
trap: days_late cannot move onto a Loan that does not exist yet; the class comes before the method.

prompt: report reads the member, the loan and the fine. Is that feature envy?

choices.text: Yes: every field it reads should move into the object it belongs to
choices.why: Then nothing would be left to combine them, and combining them is the report's job.

choices.text: No: combining several objects is what a report is for
choices.why: Right. Envy is a function mostly about one other object; report is about all of them together.

choices.text: Yes, and the fix is to make report a method of Member
choices.why: A report covers many members and loans; putting it on one member would be the misplacement.

prompt: Before replacing the switches, the section adds a test with a magazine. Why?

choices.text: None of the tests reached the else branches
choices.why: Right. The net must cover code before you move it, and books and films never took the else.

choices.text: To fix the magazine bug in the same step
choices.why: The bug is pinned and left alone; fixing it is a separate behaviour change.

choices.text: Because the library has started lending magazines this month
choices.why: No requirement arrived; the test exists to widen the net over existing code.

prompt: Run the legacy report with today = 5 April 2026 instead of 31 March. Caio's film is still out. What is the total, in cents?
hint: Only Caio's line changes: his film was due on 16 March.

prompt: Book and Film differ only in a number of days and a label. What does the section say about using classes for them?

choices.text: Classes are always better than a table, because they are open/closed
choices.why: A dictionary is open to new entries too; the section prefers it while the kinds differ only in data.

choices.text: A table would do; classes pay once a branch has real behaviour
choices.why: Right. A reference book that refuses to be lent, or a due date skipping closed days, would earn them.

choices.text: The classes were a mistake and the refactoring should be undone
choices.why: The section calls both designs legitimate; it names when each one fits.

prompt: Which of these are refactorings in Fowler's sense? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Renaming f to fine everywhere it is used
choices.why: Right. Structure changes, behaviour does not.

choices.text: Making a month with nobody late print nothing
choices.why: The output changes, so it is a behaviour change, however small.

choices.text: Moving days_late from a function onto Loan
choices.why: Right. Same answers, better home.

choices.text: Giving magazines a 7-day loan instead of none
choices.why: That fixes the pinned bug: a behaviour change with its own test.

prompt: You must add a renewal rule to report.py, and the code makes it awkward. What does the lesson suggest?

choices.text: Add the rule first and tidy up afterwards if there is time
choices.why: Tidying later rarely happens, and the awkward code makes the rule harder to get right now.

choices.text: Refactor until the change is easy, then make the easy change
choices.why: Right. Preparatory refactoring under the green tests, then the rule as a separate step with its own test.

choices.text: Rewrite report.py from scratch with the rule designed in
choices.why: A rewrite is the single large step the lesson contrasts with refactoring.

choices.text: Do both in one commit, so reviewers see the whole picture
choices.why: That wears both hats at once; neither half can be reviewed on its own.
